# TypeScript - What JavaScript gives you

Every file you have written this course is TypeScript. Today you find out what that actually
means - starting with the language underneath it.

| Already taught | Where |
|---|---|
| `let` / `const` / `var`, block scope | [week3/day2_1](/learn/w3/d2/p1) |
| Arrow functions, `async` | [week1/day5_1](/learn/w1/d5/p1) |
| `const` and dynamic vs static typing (the idea) | [week2/day2_1](/learn/w2/d2/p1) |
| Objects, arrays of objects | see the week3/week4 links in `_shared/CONCEPTS.md` |

## The eight data types

Seven **primitive**, one not. The eighth - `object` - is the one that holds the others.

| Type | Example |
|---|---|
| `string` | `"Leela"` |
| `number` | `42`, `3.14` - one type for both |
| `boolean` | `true` |
| `undefined` | declared, never assigned |
| `null` | deliberately empty |
| `bigint` | `9007199254740993n` |
| `symbol` | a guaranteed-unique key |
| **`object`** | `{}`, `[]`, functions, class instances |

`typeof` tells you which - at run time, because that is the only time JavaScript knows.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

Two answers in that output are famous mistakes and worth knowing before they bite:

| Expression | Says | Why it is odd |
|---|---|---|
| `typeof null` | `"object"` | a bug from 1995, kept for compatibility |
| `typeof []` | `"object"` | an array *is* an object; use `Array.isArray()` |

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Dynamically typed - the variable does not care

You already met this in [week2/day2_1](/learn/w2/d2/p1): a variable is a label, not a
container of a fixed shape, so the type comes from whatever value it currently holds. The
example there used `const`; the cell below shows the same freedom with `let`, since today's
point is what JavaScript allows, not which keyword to prefer.

## Where that freedom costs you

A typo does not fail. It produces `undefined`, and `undefined` keeps travelling until something
tries to use it - usually several lines away from the mistake.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

`NaN` instead of a number, and the stack trace points at the multiplication rather than at the
capital `P`. That is the single problem TypeScript was built to solve.

**Next:** [Fundamentals - The same code, in TypeScript](/learn/w7/d1/p2)

# Fundamentals - The same code, in TypeScript

TypeScript is JavaScript plus a type checker. **Every JavaScript file is already valid
TypeScript** - which is why switching a project over is mostly renaming `.js` to `.ts`.

By the end of this lesson you will have annotated variables, arrays, functions and a class,
and watched the compiler reject something the kernel happily runs.

> **Mode: Deno.** These cells run TypeScript directly. One catch, stated up front and repeated
> where it matters: **the kernel strips types and does not check them.** `npx tsc --noEmit` is the
> tool that checks. That split is the whole point of Step 6.

## Step 1 - an annotation is a colon

| JavaScript | TypeScript |
|---|---|
| `let name = "Leela"` | `let name: string = "Leela"` |
| `let count = 0` | `let count: number = 0` |
| `let ready = true` | `let ready: boolean = true` |

And most of the time you write neither, because TypeScript **infers** it.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

**Annotate what crosses a boundary** - function parameters, return types, exported values.
Let inference handle the rest; `const x: number = 1` is noise.

## Step 2 - typed arrays

| Written | Means |
|---|---|
| `string[]` | every item is a string |
| `number[]` | every item is a number |
| `(string \| number)[]` | each item is one or the other |
| `any[]` | no checking at all |

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 3 - functions: parameters and the return type

The return type goes after the parameter list. It is the annotation that catches the most bugs,
because it checks every `return` in the body at once.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 4 - classes gain types, and nothing else

You have written these since week 3. TypeScript adds annotations on the fields and the
constructor - plus `private` / `protected` / `readonly`, which JavaScript has no equivalent for.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 5 - `enum`, which JavaScript does not have

A fixed set of named values. JavaScript has no such thing, so TypeScript **generates real
JavaScript** for it - unlike an annotation, which vanishes.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

You will meet those four families for real in [day2_2](/learn/w7/d2/p2).

> A union of string literals ([week6/day1_1](/learn/w6/d1/p1)) does a similar job and
> compiles to nothing. Prefer it unless you need the value at run time, as above.

## Step 6 - the difference that actually matters

TypeScript reports mistakes at **compile time**. JavaScript reports them at **run time**, if at
all - which for a test suite means "when the test runs", and possibly not even then.

`error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'` - before anything ran.

| | JavaScript | TypeScript |
|---|---|---|
| Typo in a property name | `undefined`, discovered later | **compile error** |
| Wrong argument type | maybe works, maybe `NaN` | **compile error** |
| Needs a compile step | no | yes - but `npx playwright test` does it for you |
| Runs in a browser directly | yes | no, it is transpiled to JS first |

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 7 - `any` turns it all off

`any` means "stop checking this". It is occasionally right, usually a leak, and always worth a
second look in review - the same lesson as [week5/day5_1](/learn/w5/d5/p1).

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 8 - `import`, not `require`

| Style | Written | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| CommonJS | `const { test } = require("@playwright/test")` | older Node code |
| **ES module** | `import { test } from "@playwright/test"` | every file in this repo |

The `import` form is the one TypeScript expects, it is checkable, and it is what the
`playwright.config.ts` in this repo uses.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What happens |
|---|---|
| Annotating everything | noise; inference was already correct |
| Reaching for `any` to silence an error | the error was the useful part |
| Expecting the lesson to catch type errors | it strips types - run `npx tsc --noEmit` |
| `enum` where a string union would do | ships extra JavaScript for nothing |
| Assuming `.ts` runs in a browser | it is transpiled first |

**Next:** [Implementation - How this repo actually uses it](/learn/w7/d1/p3)

parts.title: How this repo actually uses it

blocks.text:
# Implementation - How this repo actually uses it

Same annotations, in the files you have been running for six weeks.

## Where the compiler is configured

`tsconfig.json` decides how strict TypeScript is. The two lines that matter most:

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| `"strict": true` | no implicit `any`, null checks on - **on in this repo** |
| `"types": ["node", "@playwright/test"]` | which global type packages are in scope |

`"exclude"` names files that can never satisfy this config - the Deno-targeted scripts, which use
`Deno.*` and top-level `await`. A file in the wrong runtime is not a type error to fix; it is a
file to exclude.

## Types on the boundaries, inference inside

Look at a real helper from this week. Every **parameter** and **return** is annotated; almost
nothing inside is.

| Line | Why it is annotated |
|---|---|
| `request: APIRequestContext` | it comes from outside; nothing else could infer it |
| `prefix = "w7"` | inferred `string` from the default - no annotation needed |
| `Promise<Account>` | checks every `return` in the body at once |
| `export type Account = {...}` | one name for a shape used in three files |

That is the habit: **annotate what crosses a file boundary.**

## `type` versus `interface`

Both name a shape. You will see both in real code.

| | `type` | `interface` |
|---|---|---|
| Objects | yes | yes |
| Unions (`"a" \| "b"`) | **yes** | no |
| Re-opened later to add fields | no | yes |
| What this repo uses | **`type`** | - |

Pick one per project. `type` does everything this course needs, and a union is not optional.

## Type-only imports

```ts
import { expect, type APIRequestContext } from "@playwright/test";
```

`type` in front says *this name is only a type* - so it is erased entirely and never becomes a
run-time import. It matters when importing from a file with side effects, and it documents intent
either way. Same idea you met in [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1).

## Migrating a JavaScript project

The session's claim - "rename the files and you are 99% done" - is broadly right, in this order:

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| 1 | rename `.js` to `.ts` |
| 2 | add a `tsconfig.json`, **`strict: false`** at first |
| 3 | run `npx tsc --noEmit` and fix what it finds |
| 4 | turn `strict` on and fix the next wave |
| 5 | replace each `any` as you touch that code |

Turning `strict` on at step 2 buries you in errors on day one, which is how migrations get
abandoned.

**Next:** [Practice](/learn/w7/d1/p4)

# Practice - Practice

Most of these use `npx tsc --noEmit`, because the lesson kernel cannot see a type error.
**Next:** [Day 2 - TypeScript - Prerequisites](/learn/w7/d2/p1)

problems.statement:
**Make the compiler talk**
Write a scratch `.ts` file with four deliberate errors: wrong argument type, a typo on an object
property, calling a string method on a number, and assigning to a `readonly` field.

**Right when:** `npx tsc --noEmit` reports four errors and you can name each one from its code.

**Find the NaN**
Reproduce [day1_1](/learn/w7/d1/p1)'s typo bug, then fix it by giving the object a `type`.

**Right when:** the broken version prints `NaN` and the typed version fails to compile instead.

**Type an array three ways**
Build one array as `string[]`, one as `(string | number)[]`, and one as `any[]`. Call
`.toUpperCase()` on an item of each.

**Right when:** you can say which lines the compiler stops, and which one it lets through and
why that is worse.

**Annotate a return type, break the body**
Write a function declared `: number` that returns a string in one branch.

**Right when:** the compiler catches it, and you can explain why the return annotation found a
bug that the parameter annotations could not.

**enum versus union**
Write the four status families twice - once as an `enum`, once as a string union. Then compile
both and look at what each produces.

**Right when:** you can say which one still exists at run time, and name a case where you would
need that.

**Audit `any` in this repo**
Search the week folders for `any`. For each hit, decide: necessary, or a leak?

> Hint: `JSON.parse` returns `any`, so most hits will be near a parse.

**Right when:** you have a count and a one-line verdict per hit.

**Turn strict off, then on**
Copy `tsconfig.json`, set `"strict": false`, and compile the repo. Then set it back.

**Right when:** you can name at least one thing that only `strict` catches - and say whether you
would start a new project with it on.
